messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
# Rajesh's Reckoning

Rajesh Mehta was thirty-two when the bomb went off at the downtown transit station. He had been waiting on the platform for the northbound train, reviewing notes for a therapy session scheduled that afternoon—a routine Tuesday in October that would hollow out the next five years of his life. The blast threw him backward into a concrete pillar. He remembered the sound before the pain: a crack that seemed to split the world open, followed by screaming that didn't feel human. When he regained consciousness in the hospital, his left arm was bandaged and his hearing in his right ear was diminished, but he was alive. Seventeen others were not.

In the months after, Rajesh had returned to his practice at the community mental health clinic with what he believed was resilience. His wife, Priya, was relieved to have him back at work. His colleagues remarked on his composure. But something fundamental had shifted in how he moved through the world. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt absolute, that he could not prevent terrible things from happening—not to himself, not to anyone. The bomb had taught him that control was an illusion, that safety was a story people told themselves. The man he had been before October—the one who believed in the efficacy of talk therapy, in the possibility of change through insight and effort—felt like someone else entirely, someone naïve and foolish.

The nighttime became unbearable first. Rajesh would lie awake beside Priya, unable to sleep, his mind cycling through scenarios of catastrophe. When exhaustion finally pulled him under, he would jolt awake in the dark, his body flooded with adrenaline, certain that something was coming. He began leaving lights on throughout the house. When Priya asked him to turn them off, he couldn't explain the panic that rose in his throat at the prospect of darkness. He had started drinking bourbon most nights—just enough to blunt the edge, to make sleep possible. It had become a ritual, something he depended on. Loud noises sent him reeling. A car backfiring on the street outside his office caused him to drop a pen and grip the armrest of his chair so hard his knuckles whitened. His patients noticed. One had asked if he was all right. The question had mortified him. He was supposed to be the stable presence in the room, the one who held space for others' suffering. Instead, he was barely holding himself together. His startle response had become so pronounced that even the notification sound on his phone could send his heart racing, his palms slick with sweat.

By thirty-seven, Rajesh had begun avoiding anything that felt remotely unpredictable or stressful. He turned down invitations to social events, canceled standing plans with friends, stopped attending the community temple where he and Priya had been married. He told himself these things were unnecessary, that they were just sources of potential threat. His world had contracted to a narrow corridor: home, the clinic, the drive between them. Even at work, he had begun to limit his caseload, referring away patients with trauma histories because their stories triggered a vertigo he couldn't manage. He sat through sessions feeling distant from his own profession, as if watching himself perform the role of psychologist from behind glass. The consequences had become undeniable. His supervisor had gently suggested he consider a leave of absence; the clinic director had expressed concern about his declining patient load and the impact on the department's capacity. Priya had stopped inviting her sister over for dinner, had stopped mentioning gatherings with her family, had learned to move through their home as though navigating around his invisible boundaries.

The alcohol had escalated. A glass of bourbon became two, then a third. Priya had found him asleep on the couch at nine in the evening more than once, an empty bottle on the side table. She had asked him, gently at first and then with visible frustration, what was happening to him. He couldn't answer. How could he tell her that the person she had married—the thoughtful, engaged man who had wanted to help people heal—had been replaced by someone hollow and afraid, someone who spent half his day in a dissociative fog, drifting into fantasy scenarios where he had somehow changed that October morning, where he had taken a different train, where the bomb had never been built? It was Priya who finally insisted he seek help. She had found him researching substances on his laptop at three in the morning, his speech slurred, his pupils dilated. She had wept, not from anger but from grief—grief for the man he had been, for the marriage that was slowly becoming a careful choreography around his avoidance. Rajesh had resisted at first. How could he, a psychologist, admit to needing therapy? But the weight of his own unrecognizability had become too much. He was no longer certain who he was or what he was capable of. He was terrified of the darkness, of loud noises, of sudden sounds, of the possibility that at any moment, without warning, everything could shatter again. And he was more afraid still of the person he was becoming in his attempts to outrun that terror.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Age discrepancy: Patient is 37, but vignette states Rajesh was 32 at the time of the bombing and is now 37, which would make the bombing only 5 years ago. However, the vignette also states 'five years of his life' were hollowed out, creating internal consistency but the current age context is ambiguous in the present narrative.: The vignette contains an internal timeline issue that makes the age validation unclear. While it states Rajesh was 32 at the bombing and is now 37, the narrative voice and present-tense descriptions suggest the current timeframe, but this is not explicitly confirmed.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.

# Rajesh's Reckoning

Rajesh Mehta was thirty-two when the bomb went off at the downtown transit station. He had been waiting on the platform for the northbound train, reviewing notes for a therapy session scheduled that afternoon—a routine Tuesday in October that would hollow out the next five years of his life. The blast threw him backward into a concrete pillar. He remembered the sound before the pain: a crack that seemed to split the world open, followed by screaming that didn't feel human. When he regained consciousness in the hospital, his left arm was bandaged and his hearing in his right ear was diminished, but he was alive. Seventeen others were not. Now, at thirty-seven, Rajesh sat in the waiting room of another therapist's office—a role reversal that felt like a confession of failure—and tried to remember what it had been like to believe that understanding yourself could change your life.

In the months after the bombing, Rajesh had returned to his practice at the community mental health clinic with what he believed was resilience. His wife, Priya, was relieved to have him back at work. His colleagues remarked on his composure. But something fundamental had shifted in how he moved through the world. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt absolute, that he could not prevent terrible things from happening—not to himself, not to anyone. The bomb had taught him that control was an illusion, that safety was a story people told themselves. The man he had been before October—the one who believed in the efficacy of talk therapy, in the possibility of change through insight and effort—felt like someone else entirely, someone naïve and foolish. What frightened him most was the randomness of it all. He had done nothing to deserve being on that platform at that moment. He had not chosen poorly or failed to prepare. A bomb had simply existed in the world, and his body had been in its path. There was no logic to survive, no moral framework that made sense of why he had walked away when others had not.

The nighttime became unbearable first. Rajesh would lie awake beside Priya, unable to sleep, his mind cycling through scenarios of catastrophe. When exhaustion finally pulled him under, he would jolt awake in the dark, his body flooded with adrenaline, certain that something was coming. He began leaving lights on throughout the house. When Priya asked him to turn them off, he couldn't explain the panic that rose in his throat at the prospect of darkness. He had started drinking bourbon most nights—just enough to blunt the edge, to make sleep possible. It had become a ritual, something he depended on. Loud noises sent him reeling. A car backfiring on the street outside his office caused him to drop a pen and grip the armrest of his chair so hard his knuckles whitened. His patients noticed. One had asked if he was all right. The question had mortified him. He was supposed to be the stable presence in the room, the one who held space for others' suffering. Instead, he was barely holding himself together. His startle response had become so pronounced that even the notification sound on his phone could send his heart racing, his palms slick with sweat. The worst part was that he couldn't control it. His body had learned something his mind couldn't unlearn: that danger was everywhere, that the next sound could be the one that changed everything, that vigilance was the only honest response to a world that could detonate without warning.

By thirty-seven, Rajesh had begun avoiding anything that felt remotely unpredictable or stressful. He turned down invitations to social events, canceled standing plans with friends, stopped attending the community temple where he and Priya had been married. He told himself these things were unnecessary, that they were just sources of potential threat. His world had contracted to a narrow corridor: home, the clinic, the drive between them. Even at work, he had begun to limit his caseload, referring away patients with trauma histories because their stories triggered a vertigo he couldn't manage. He sat through sessions feeling distant from his own profession, as if watching himself perform the role of psychologist from behind glass. The consequences had become undeniable. His supervisor had gently suggested he consider a leave of absence; the clinic director had expressed concern about his declining patient load and the impact on the department's capacity. Priya had stopped inviting her sister over for dinner, had stopped mentioning gatherings with her family, had learned to move through their home as though navigating around his invisible boundaries. She had also stopped asking him to come to bed at a reasonable hour. Instead, she would find him on the couch at nine in the evening, an empty glass of bourbon on the side table, his breathing shallow and even. The alcohol had escalated. A glass became two, then a third. Some nights he would wake on the couch with no memory of how he had gotten there, his mouth dry, his thoughts fragmented and confused. Other nights he didn't wake at all—Priya would simply cover him with a blanket and retreat to their bedroom alone.

The turning point came when Priya found him at three in the morning, researching substances on his laptop, his speech slurred and his pupils dilated in a way that frightened her. She had wept, not from anger but from grief—grief for the man she had married, for the marriage that was slowly becoming a careful choreography around his avoidance. Rajesh had resisted the idea of seeking help at first. How could he, a psychologist, admit to needing therapy? But something in Priya's face that night—a kind of resignation, as if she were grieving someone who was still alive—had broken through his resistance. Now, at thirty-seven, five years after the bomb had taught him that the world was fundamentally unsafe, he sat in a therapist's waiting room and tried to explain to himself why he had come. He was terrified of the darkness, of loud noises, of sudden sounds, of the possibility that at any moment, without warning, everything could shatter again. And he was more afraid still of the person he was becoming in his attempts to outrun that terror—the hollow man, the absent husband, the psychologist who no longer believed in the possibility of healing, least of all for himself.
